legend: Schematic overview of CDC73 gene aberrancies and associated genomic hallmarks in parathyroid carcinoma. Positioned at chromosome 1q25-q31, the CDC73 gene locus recurrently exhibits loss of heterozygosity in parathyroid carcinoma, in addition to gene mutations occurring most frequently in exons 1, 2, and 7. At the pangenomic level, CDC73-mutated parathyroid carcinomas display a higher mutation burden, more copy-number alterations, and poorer patient outcomes than CDC73-wildtype cases.

Parafibromin (PFIB) exhibits numerous tumour-suppressor functions in the cell. As a member of the RNA polymerase II–associated factor (PAF) complex, parafibromin is required for mRNA elongation and quality control processes, and it also controls the expression of the proto-oncogenes CCND1 (encoding cyclin D1) and MYC via epigenetic mechanisms. Upon loss of parafibromin, these processes are dysregulated, which in turn has been associated with cell-cycle activation and increased proliferative ability.

A focus of angioinvasion characterized by intravascular tumour cells admixed with fibrin/thrombus. Vascular invasion (angioinvasion) is typically assessed at the tumour periphery or at the tumour capsule, but not within the tumour substance.
Local gross nodular invasion into the adjacent soft tissue. The tumour also showed angioinvasion (not shown here).
Tumour invades the thyroid parenchyma.
Broad sheets of tumour nests separated by thin fibrotic bands. The tumour also showed angioinvasion in a separate section.
Fibrous bands in parathyroid carcinoma. However, this finding alone does not warrant the diagnosis of malignancy.

The triad of high-risk histopathological features comprises foci of coagulative tumour necrosis in association with prominent macronucleoli and increased mitotic activity (> 5 mitoses/10 mm2). Inset: High magnification showing mitosis.

legend: Cytomorphological features of a parafibromin-immunodeficient tumour. The tumour is enriched in oncocytic cells with perinuclear clearing. This morphology is not specific to parathyroid carcinoma; the identification of invasive growth is required to render the morphological diagnosis of parathyroid carcinoma.

Parafibromin immunohistochemistry. Loss of nuclear parafibromin expression has been regarded as a reliable biomarker of malignancy in the appropriate morphological setting. This photomicrograph shows loss of nuclear parafibromin expression in a morphologically diagnosed parathyroid carcinoma. Note that the intratumoural endothelial cells, which serve as an internal control, show retained nuclear parafibromin reactivity.
Diffuse strong PGP9.5 expression in a locally invasive parathyroid carcinoma. Unlike adenomas, parathyroid carcinomas may show PGP9.5 expression.
Unlike in adenomas, loss of expression of APC can feature in parathyroid carcinoma. Note that non-tumorous (endothelial) cells remain positive for APC.
BCL2 immunohistochemistry. Unlike adenomas, parathyroid carcinomas can feature reduced to absent BCL2 expression. This photomicrograph shows near-global loss of expression of BCL2.
P27 immunohistochemistry. Parathyroid carcinoma with loss of nuclear expression of p27. Note that the endothelial cells retain nuclear p27 expression.

legend: The application of phosphohistone H3 immunohistochemistry can be used to facilitate an objective mitotic count in parathyroid neoplasms. Green circles highlight mitotic figures in this photomicrograph.
Ki-67 immunohistochemistry. Most parathyroid carcinomas show a Ki-67 labelling index > 5%. This photomicrograph illustrates an increased Ki-67 proliferation index from a parathyroid carcinoma.
CD34 immunohistochemistry can be used to highlight vascular spaces in angioinvasive parathyroid carcinomas.
GATA3 is expressed in normal and neoplastic parathyroid tissue. This photomicrograph illustrates GATA3 expression in a parathyroid carcinoma with angioinvasion.
PTH is expressed in normal and neoplastic parathyroid tissue. This photomicrograph illustrates PTH expression in a parathyroid carcinoma with angioinvasion.
In angioinvasive parathyroid carcinomas, intravascular tumour and fibrin/platelet complex can be highlighted using CD61 immunohistochemistry.
